messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj is a 61-year-old South Asian man who worked as a paramedic for nearly three decades. Four years ago, he responded to a hazardous materials call at a chemical warehouse. Inside a dim, cavernous storage bay—the lights had shorted out—he crawled through a dark corridor to reach an unconscious worker. As he moved, a sharp, sweet smell like cheap vodka filled his respirator; the seal had cracked. He inhaled a solvent-laden vapor and felt his throat seize, his lungs burning. For several minutes, he genuinely believed he would die there, alone in the dark, until a colleague dragged him out. At the hospital, he was decontaminated and eventually discharged, but the terror never left.

Now any encounter with that sweet, alcoholic odor—a colleague’s hand sanitizer, a spilled drink at a party—instantly hurls him back into the warehouse. The same suffocating panic returns, so overwhelming that he has to stop whatever he is doing, gripping a counter until his knuckles whiten. This happens without warning: he can be walking through a parking garage after dusk, and the darkness alone is enough to conjure the full memory, complete with the burning in his throat. After the memory had taken hold, he found himself noticing any dark or enclosed space as a potential trigger, scanning for the sweet smell even when none was present. Over the months, these unbidden flashbacks have led him to develop a rigid set of strategies. He avoids hospitals altogether, stepping out of the ambulance bay before a call ends and asking his partner to handle any transport. He has also stopped attending his own annual physicals—he simply cancels them. To keep the memories at bay, he constantly surrounds himself with people. He joins his coworkers for every after-shift meal, invites neighbors over for late-night tea, and spends weekends at crowded temples or shopping malls. “If I’m alone even for a minute,” he told his wife, “my mind starts replaying it—how I could have prevented it, if I’d checked the mask seal.” This rumination about prevention is itself a trap: the more he tries to mentally rewrite the event, the more vivid and terrifying the memory becomes, so he redoubles his socializing to drown it out.

But his constant socializing also creates new triggers. At a recent family dinner, someone accidentally knocked over a bottle of whiskey, and the smell hit him before he could look away—the full memory detonated. He had to leave the table, humiliated, and later that night he lay awake ruminating. The more he avoids medical settings, the more vigilant he becomes for any sign of chemical smells, so that even a dark corner of his own garage—a space he now keeps brightly lit—feels menacing. His wife has grown frustrated that he is never home, and his paramedic supervisor has noticed his refusal to set foot inside the emergency department. The avoidance itself reinforces the idea that hospitals are dangerous, making the triggers even more potent.

Now, after a near-panic attack during a mandatory retinal exam—the darkened room, the faint antiseptic smell—Raj has finally agreed to seek help. He is terrified that his career, his marriage, and his health are all slipping away. He hopes that therapy might give him a way to be alone with his thoughts without being consumed by them, and to walk into a hospital without feeling like he is suffocating again.
